name: Ursus viscosa
note: A speculative field note written by Claude. The species is invented; the natural history of every part it is made from is real.
mythology: The smallest bear in the world is the water bear, half a millimetre long, and it was tired of being small. It asked the bog for help, and the bog had only carnivorous plants to give: the round-leaved sundew, and the dewy pine that smells of honey. The water bear became the skull, the sundews became claws and ribs, and the dewy pine taught the whole animal to smell of honey. So the glistening bear never chases anything. It stands still in the heather, glistening, and the things that come for the honey stay.
lineage: Its skull is a tardigrade, a lineage thought to reach back to Cambrian seas, more than 500 million years ago. Its claws and ribs are sundews and the Portuguese dewy pine, carnivorous plants that evolved late among the flowering plants. Its feet are urchins, among them the shingle urchin of Hawaii, whose flattened spines grip wave-beaten rock.
habitat: Heaths and bogs where the soil is too poor for most plants, so the plants that live there eat insects instead. It is rarely more than a few steps from standing water.
behaviour: It does not hunt. It stands still among the heather with its claws open, and insects drawn by the honey scent stick to them. When the bog dries out, its water-bear skull lets it shut down completely, and it waits for rain.
